keyVerseText: Of the sons of Hashum; Mattenai, Mattathah, Zabad, Eliphelet, Jeremai, Manasseh, and Shimei.
rootMeaning: The name מַתְּנַי (Mattᵉnay) derives from the root מַתָּן (mattân), which means 'gift' or 'to give.' This root conveys the idea of a generous bestowal or reward, emphasizing the concept of a divine or gracious gift. Understanding Mattᵉnay as 'gift of Jehovah' highlights that the name itself carries a theological nuance of God’s providential giving, beyond simply being a proper noun.
usageInScripture: The word מַתְּנַי appears three times in the Hebrew Scriptures, consistently as a proper name transliterated as 'Mattenai.' It refers to three distinct Israelites: a priest during the time of Joiakim and two men mentioned in Ezra who put away foreign wives. This consistent usage as a personal name underscores its role in identifying specific individuals, while its root meaning enriches the understanding of their identity as linked to God's gift or provision.
theologicalSignificance: Recognizing מַתְּנַי as 'gift of Jehovah' invites believers to see the individuals bearing this name as reflections of God’s gracious giving to His people. It reminds us that every person and role within the community of faith is ultimately a gift from God, appointed for His purposes. This perspective encourages a humble acknowledgment of God’s sovereignty and generosity in the lives of His servants. Moreover, the fact that two bearers of this name are involved in covenantal faithfulness by putting away foreign wives points to the importance of holiness and obedience as responses to God’s gifts.
keyVerseReflection: Ezra 10:33 lists Mattenai among the sons of Hashum, situating him within a community committed to covenant renewal. The presence of the name here, meaning 'gift of Jehovah,' subtly affirms that this individual is part of God’s gracious provision for the restoration of Israel. It highlights the continuity of God’s faithful gifts through His people even in times of reform and renewal.
